\chapter{Chapter08 — Biased Analysis}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from FABL.Chapter08.BiasedAnalysis
\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{FABL.Chapter08.BiasedAnalysis}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Bias complement]
\lean{FABL.biasComplement}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b004
}
\label{FABL.biasComplement}
\leanok
For a real number $p$, define its bias complement to be $1-p$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Bias mean]
\lean{FABL.biasMean}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b004
}
\label{FABL.biasMean}
\leanok
For a real number $p$, define its bias mean to be $1-2p$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Bias variance scale]
\lean{FABL.biasVarianceScale}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b004}
\label{FABL.biasVarianceScale}
\leanok
For a real number $p$, define its bias variance scale to be $4p(1-p)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Bias standard deviation]
\lean{FABL.biasSigma}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b004}
\label{FABL.biasSigma}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasVarianceScale}
For a real number $p$, define its bias standard deviation to be the nonnegative square
root of $4p(1-p)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Range of the bias mean]
\lean{FABL.biasMean_mem_Icc}
\label{FABL.biasMean_mem_Icc}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasMean}
\difficulty{3}
For every $p\in[0,1]$, the bias mean $1-2p$ lies in $[-1,1]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of the bias variance scale]
\lean{FABL.biasVarianceScale_nonneg}
\label{FABL.biasVarianceScale_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasVarianceScale}
\difficulty{3}
For every real number $p\in[0,1]$, the bias variance scale $4p(1-p)$ is nonnegative.
\end{theorem}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b002}
For every real number $p$ with $0\le p\le1$, the square of the square root of $4p(1-p)$
equals $4p(1-p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Positivity of the bias scale]
\lean{FABL.biasSigma_pos}
\label{FABL.biasSigma_pos}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasSigma, FABL.biasVarianceScale}
\difficulty{3}
For every real number $p$ with $0<p<1$, the square root of $4p(1-p)$ is positive.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Biased sign distribution]
\lean{FABL.biasedSignPMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p017-b007,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b004
}
\label{FABL.biasedSignPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasMean_mem_Icc, FABL.coordinateNoisePMF}
For $p\in[0,1]$, let $\mu_p$ be the probability mass function on the two signs obtained
from the one-coordinate noise distribution with the bias associated with $p$.
\end{definition}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b002}
For every $p\in[0,1]$, the biased sign probability mass at $+1$ equals the correlation
keep probability associated with the bias mean $1-2p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Real mass of a biased sign]
\lean{FABL.biasedSignPMF_apply_toReal}
\label{FABL.biasedSignPMF_apply_toReal}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasMean_mem_Icc, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.biasedSignPMF_apply_neg_one, FABL.biasedSignPMF_apply_one, FABL.correlationKeepProbability, FABL.correlationKeepProbability_le_one}
\difficulty{5}
For every $p\in[0,1]$ and every sign $x\in\{\pm1\}$, the real-valued mass of $x$ under
the biased sign distribution is $1-p$ if $x=+1$, and is $p$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Full support of the biased sign distribution]
\lean{FABL.biasedSignPMF_hasFullSupport}
\label{FABL.biasedSignPMF_hasFullSupport}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.PMFHasFullSupport, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.biasedSignPMF_apply_toReal}
\difficulty{4}
For every $p\in(0,1)$, the biased sign distribution assigns nonzero mass to every sign
in $\{\pm1\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mean of a biased sign]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedSignPMF_signValue}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedSignPMF_signValue}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasMean_mem_Icc, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_coordinateNoisePMF_signValue, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{1}
Let $p\in[0,1]$, and choose a sign $X\in\{-1,1\}$ according to the probability
distribution with mean $1-2p$. Then the expected value of $X$ is $1-2p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Standardized biased sign]
\lean{FABL.biasedStandardizedSign}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b004}
\label{FABL.biasedStandardizedSign}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasSigma, FABL.signValue}
For $p\in\mathbb{R}$ and a sign $x\in\{-1,+1\}$, define its standardized value to be
$(x-(1-2p))/\sigma(p)$, where $\sigma(p)$ is the bias standard deviation.
\end{definition}

divided by the bias standard deviation.

\begin{theorem}[Biased standardized sign one eq sqrt]
\lean{FABL.biasedStandardizedSign_one_eq_sqrt}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b004}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b002}
Let $0<p<1$, and choose a sign $X\in\{-1,1\}$ according to the probability distribution
with mean $1-2p$. Write $\sigma=\sqrt{4p(1-p)}$ and $Z=(X-(1-2p))/\sigma$. Then the
expected value of $Z$ is $0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Second moment of the standardized sign]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedStandardizedSign_sq}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedStandardizedSign_sq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasSigma, FABL.biasSigma_pos, FABL.biasSigma_sq, FABL.biasVarianceScale, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.biasedSignPMF_apply_toReal, FABL.biasedStandardizedSign, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.signValue_neg_one, FABL.signValue_one}
\difficulty{5}
Let $0<p<1$, and choose a sign $X\in\{-1,1\}$ according to the probability distribution
with mean $1-2p$. Write $\sigma=\sqrt{4p(1-p)}$ and $Z=(X-(1-2p))/\sigma$. Then the
expected value of $Z^2$ is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Biased site Fourier function]
\lean{FABL.biasedSiteFourierFunction}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p221-b002}
\label{FABL.biasedSiteFourierFunction}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasedStandardizedSign}
For $p\in\mathbb{R}$, $j\in\{0,1\}$, and a sign $x\in\{-1,+1\}$, define the site
function to equal $1$ when $j=0$ and the biased-standardized sign of $x$ at bias $p$
when $j=1$.
\end{definition}

  {FABL.biasedView_apply}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b003}
For every $p\in(0,1)$ and indices $a,b\in\{0,1\}$, the expectation under the biased sign
distribution of the product of the corresponding biased site Fourier functions is $1$
when $a=b$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Biased site Fourier basis]
\lean{FABL.biasedSiteBasis}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p221-b001}
\label{FABL.biasedSiteBasis}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasedSiteFourierFunction, FABL.biasedSiteFourierFunction_orthonormal, FABL.linearIndependent_of_pmf_orthonormal}
For each real number $p$ with $0<p<1$, the two biased site Fourier functions on the sign
space $\{-1,1\}$ form a basis over $\mathbb{R}$ of all real-valued functions on that
space.
\end{definition}

the corresponding biased site Fourier function.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Biased site Fourier basis]
\lean{FABL.biasedSiteFourierBasis}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p221-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p221-b002
}
\label{FABL.biasedSiteFourierBasis}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteFourierBasis, FABL.Sign, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.biasedSiteBasis, FABL.biasedSiteBasis_apply, FABL.biasedSiteFourierFunction, FABL.biasedSiteFourierFunction_orthonormal}
For $p\in(0,1)$, the biased site basis is an orthonormal basis of the real-valued
functions on the two-sign space under expectation with respect to the sign distribution
biased by $p$. Its index $0$ vector is the constant function $1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Subset multi-index]
\lean{FABL.subsetMultiIndex}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p221-b002}
\label{FABL.subsetMultiIndex}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.MultiIndex}
For a subset $S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, define its multi-index on the coordinates by
assigning index $1$ to coordinates in $S$ and index $0$ to all other coordinates.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Zero coordinates of a subset index]
\lean{FABL.subsetMultiIndex_eq_zero_iff}
\label{FABL.subsetMultiIndex_eq_zero_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.subsetMultiIndex}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$, subset $S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, and
$i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, the subset index associated with $S$ has value zero at $i$ if
and only if $i\notin S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Injectivity of subset indices]
\lean{FABL.subsetMultiIndex_injective}
\label{FABL.subsetMultiIndex_injective}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.subsetMultiIndex}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$, the map sending a finite subset
$S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ to the index that takes value $1$ on $S$ and $0$ outside
$S$ is injective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Support of a Subset Multi-Index]
\lean{FABL.signMultiIndexSupport_subsetMultiIndex}
\label{FABL.signMultiIndexSupport_subsetMultiIndex}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.multiIndexSupport, FABL.signMultiIndexSupport, FABL.subsetMultiIndex}
\difficulty{1}
For every $n\in\mathbb N$ and every subset $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the support of
the multi-index that takes value $1$ on $S$ and $0$ off $S$ is exactly $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Support recovers the subset index]
\lean{FABL.subsetMultiIndex_signMultiIndexSupport}
\label{FABL.subsetMultiIndex_signMultiIndexSupport}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.MultiIndex, FABL.multiIndexSupport, FABL.signMultiIndexSupport, FABL.subsetMultiIndex}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$ and every function $a:\mathrm{Fin}(n)\to\mathrm{Fin}(2)$,
the index that is $1$ on the support of $a$ (the coordinates where $a$ is nonzero) and
$0$ elsewhere equals $a$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Subsets and binary multi-indices]
\lean{FABL.finsetEquivBinaryMultiIndex}
\label{FABL.finsetEquivBinaryMultiIndex}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.MultiIndex, FABL.signMultiIndexSupport, FABL.signMultiIndexSupport_subsetMultiIndex, FABL.subsetMultiIndex, FABL.subsetMultiIndex_signMultiIndexSupport}
For each natural number $n$, the subsets of $\in{n}$ are in bijection with functions
from $\in{n}$ to $\in{2}$, by recording the binary membership value at each coordinate.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Biased monomial]
\lean{FABL.biasedMonomial}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p221-b002}
\label{FABL.biasedMonomial}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteFourierBasis.productFunction, FABL.biasedSiteFourierBasis, FABL.subsetMultiIndex}
Let $p\in(0,1)$, let $S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, and let $x\in\{-1,+1\}^n$. The biased
monomial indexed by $S$ is the product-basis function associated with the multi-index
that is $1$ on $S$ and $0$ elsewhere, evaluated at $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Biased Fourier coefficient]
\lean{FABL.biasedFourierCoeff}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p221-b002}
\label{FABL.biasedFourierCoeff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteFourierBasis.fourierCoeff, FABL.biasedSiteFourierBasis, FABL.subsetMultiIndex}
Let $p\in(0,1)$, let $f\colon\{-1,+1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, and let
$S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. The biased Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S$ is its
coefficient in the product basis indexed by the multi-index that is $1$ on $S$ and $0$
elsewhere.
\end{definition}

  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p207-b005}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $p\in(0,1)$, let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$, and
let $S$ be a set of coordinates. The biased Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S$ equals the
expectation of the product of $f$ and the biased monomial associated to $S$, under the
product distribution with bias parameter $p$.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.biasedView}
  {context}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b003,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b002}
\proofstep
  {FABL.biasedView_apply}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b003,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b002}
Let $0<p<1$, let $i$ be a coordinate, and let $x\in\{\pm1\}^n$. With $\mu=1-2p$,
$\sigma=\sqrt{4p(1-p)}$, and the biased monomial defined using the associated
one-coordinate Fourier basis, the sign at coordinate $i$ satisfies
$x_i=\mu+\sigma\,\chi_{\{i\}}(x)$.
\end{theorem}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p207-b005}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $p\in(0,1)$, let $i$ be a coordinate, and let $S$
be a set of coordinates. The biased Fourier coefficient at $S$ of the function that
returns the sign in coordinate $i$ is the bias mean $1-2p$ if $S$ is empty, the bias
standard deviation $\sqrt{4p(1-p)}$ if $S=\{i\}$, and zero otherwise.
\end{theorem}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b002}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $p\in(0,1)$, and let $i$ be a coordinate. The
biased Fourier coefficient at the empty set of the function that returns the sign in
coordinate $i$ equals the bias mean $1-2p$.
\end{theorem}

  {context}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b003,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b002}
\proofstep
  {FABL.biasedView_apply}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b003,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b002}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $p\in(0,1)$, and let $i$ be a coordinate. The
biased Fourier coefficient at $\{i\}$ of the function that returns the sign in
coordinate $i$ equals the bias standard deviation $\sqrt{4p(1-p)}$.
\end{theorem}

  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p207-b002}
\proofstep
  {FABL.biasedView_apply}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p207-b002}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $p\in(0,1)$, let $i$ be a coordinate, and let $S$
be a nonempty set of coordinates different from $\{i\}$. The biased Fourier coefficient
at $S$ of the function that returns the sign in coordinate $i$ is zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Biased view of a cube function]
\lean{FABL.biasedView}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b002}
\label{FABL.biasedView}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.ProductL2, FABL.Sign}
For a natural number $n$, a real parameter $p$ with $0<p<1$, and a real-valued function
$f$ on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, its biased view is the function on $n$-tuples of
signs given by the same values as $f$.
\end{definition}

  {FABL.biasedView}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b002}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $p$ be a real number with $0<p<1$, and let $f$ be a
real-valued function on sign vectors of length $n$. For every such vector $x$, the
biased view of $f$ at $x$ equals $f(x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Selection function on three signs]
\lean{FABL.selectionFunction}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p221-b005}
\label{FABL.selectionFunction}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign}
For a point $x=(x_0,x_1,x_2)$ in the three-dimensional sign cube, define a sign by
taking $x_1$ when $x_0=-1$ and taking $x_2$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

  {FABL.selectionFunction}
  {direct}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p221-b005}
Let $p\in(0,1)$ and $x\in\{−1,1\}^3$. For each subset $S\subseteq\{0,1,2\}$, write
$M_S^p(x)$ for the biased Fourier product monomial indexed by $S$. The value of the
selection function at $x$ is $1-2p$ plus
$\frac{1-(1-2p)}{2}\sqrt{4p(1-p)}\,M_{\{1\}}^p(x)+\frac{1+(1-2p)}{2}\sqrt{4p(1-p)}\,M_{\{2\}}^p(x)-\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\sqrt{4p(1-p)}\bigr)^2M_{\{0,1\}}^p(x)+\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\sqrt{4p(1-p)}\bigr)^2M_{\{0,2\}}^p(x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Biased discrete derivative]
\lean{FABL.biasedDiscreteDerivative}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b004
}
\label{FABL.biasedDiscreteDerivative}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasSigma, FABL.setCoordinate}
Let $n$ be a natural number, $p\in\mathbb R$, $i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, and
$f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$. For each $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, define the biased discrete
derivative of $f$ in coordinate $i$ by $D_i^{(p)}f(x)=\beta_p\bigl(f(x^{i\to
1})-f(x^{i\to -1})\bigr)/2$, where $x^{i\to a}$ is obtained by setting coordinate $i$ of
$x$ to $a$ and $\beta_p$ denotes the bias normalization factor.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Biased derivative as a scaled derivative]
\lean{FABL.biasedDiscreteDerivative_eq_sigma_mul}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b004
}

  {FABL.biasedDiscreteDerivative}
  {direct}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b004}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $p\in\mathbb R$, let $i$ be one of the $n$ coordinates,
and let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\mathbb R$. The biased discrete derivative of $f$ in coordinate
$i$ is the function obtained by multiplying its ordinary discrete derivative by the
square root of $4p(1-p)$ at every point of the cube.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Difference of standardized signs]
\lean{FABL.biasSigma_mul_standardizedSign_difference_div_two}
\label{FABL.biasSigma_mul_standardizedSign_difference_div_two}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasSigma, FABL.biasSigma_pos, FABL.biasedStandardizedSign, FABL.biasedStandardizedSign_neg_one_eq, FABL.biasedStandardizedSign_one_eq}
\difficulty{3}
For a real number $p$ with $0<p<1$, let $\sigma_p$ be the square root of $4p(1-p)$ and
let the standardized value of a sign $s\in\{\pm1\}$ be $(s-(1-2p))/\sigma_p$. Then
$\sigma_p$ times the difference between the standardized values at $1$ and $-1$, divided
by $2$, equals $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Derivative of a biased monomial]
\lean{FABL.biasedDiscreteDerivative_biasedMonomial}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b005}
\label{FABL.biasedDiscreteDerivative_biasedMonomial}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasSigma, FABL.biasSigma_mul_standardizedSign_difference_div_two, FABL.biasedDiscreteDerivative, FABL.biasedMonomial, FABL.biasedMonomial_apply, FABL.biasedStandardizedSign, FABL.setCoordinate, FABL.setCoordinate_apply_of_ne, FABL.setCoordinate_apply_self}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $p\in(0,1)$, let $i$ be a coordinate in
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $x\in\{\pm1\}^n$. The biased
discrete derivative of the biased monomial indexed by $S$, evaluated at $x$ in
coordinate $i$, equals the biased monomial indexed by $S\setminus\{i\}$ at $x$ if $i\in
S$, and equals $0$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

  {direct}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b004}
\proofstep
  {FABL.biasSigma_mul_standardizedSign_difference_div_two}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b004}
\proofstep
  {FABL.biasedDiscreteDerivative_biasedMonomial}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b005}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $p\in(0,1)$, let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\mathbb R$, let $i$ be
one of the $n$ coordinates, and let $x\in\{\pm1\}^n$. The biased discrete derivative of
$f$ in coordinate $i$ at $x$ equals the sum, over all subsets $S$ of the coordinates
containing $i$, of the biased Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S$ times the biased
monomial indexed by $S\setminus\{i\}$ evaluated at $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation under a biased sign distribution]
\lean{FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedSignPMF}
\label{FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedSignPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.biasedSignPMF_apply_toReal, FABL.pmfExpectation}
\difficulty{3}
Let $p\in(0,1)$ and let $g$ be a real-valued function on the two signs. Under the sign
distribution that assigns probability $1-p$ to $1$ and probability $p$ to $-1$, its
expectation is $(1-p)g(1)+pg(-1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Conditional variance of a biased Boolean function]
\lean{FABL.coordinateConditionalVariance_biasedSignPMF_toReal}
\label{FABL.coordinateConditionalVariance_biasedSignPMF_toReal}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.biasSigma, FABL.biasSigma_sq, FABL.biasVarianceScale, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.coordinateConditionalVariance, FABL.flipCoordinate, FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedSignPMF, FABL.replaceCoordinate, FABL.setCoordinate, FABL.setCoordinate_eq_self}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $p\in(0,1)$, and let $f:\{−1,1\}^n\to\{−1,1\}$ be a Boolean
function. For every coordinate $i$ and input $x$, the variance of the real-valued
function $f$ when coordinate $i$ is resampled from the biased sign law that assigns
probability $p$ to $-1$ and $1-p$ to $1$ is $4p(1-p)$ if $f(x)$ changes when coordinate
$i$ is flipped, and is $0$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Biased coordinate flip probability]
\lean{FABL.biasedFlipProbability}
\label{FABL.biasedFlipProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.flipCoordinate, FABL.productMean}
Let $p\in(0,1)$, let $f$ map the sign cube on $n$ coordinates to the two-element sign
group, and let $i$ be a coordinate. The biased flip probability is the probability,
under the product sign distribution with bias $p$, that flipping coordinate $i$ changes
the value of $f$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{3}
\proofstep
  {FABL.Sign}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p014-b002,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p018-b002}
\proofstep

\proofstep
  {FABL.biasedFlipProbability}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p046-b002,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b002}
Let $p\in(0,1)$, let $f$ be a function from the $n$-dimensional sign cube to the two
signs, and let $i$ be a coordinate. Under the product distribution with bias parameter
$p$, the influence of the real-valued sign representation of $f$ at $i$ equals $4p(1-p)$
times the probability that flipping coordinate $i$ changes the value of $f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Pointwise sensitivity]
\lean{FABL.biasedSensitivity}
\label{FABL.biasedSensitivity}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.flipCoordinate}
For a function $f$ from the sign cube on $n$ coordinates to the two-element sign group
and a point $x$ in that cube, the sensitivity of $f$ at $x$ is the number of coordinates
whose individual flip changes the value of $f$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Sensitivity as a sum of indicators]
\lean{FABL.biasedSensitivity_cast}
\label{FABL.biasedSensitivity_cast}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedSensitivity, FABL.flipCoordinate}
\difficulty{3}
For a sign-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional sign cube and an input $x$, the
real-valued sensitivity at $x$ equals the sum over coordinates of the indicator that
flipping that coordinate changes the value of $f$.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.biasedSensitivity}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p017-b008,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p046-b002}
\proofstep
  {FABL.biasedSensitivity_cast}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p017-b008,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p046-b002}
Let $p\in(0,1)$ and let $f$ be a function from the sign cube on $n$ coordinates to
$\{\pm1\}$. Under the product distribution in which each coordinate has bias
parameter $p$, the total influence of the real-valued sign representation of $f$ equals
$4p(1-p)$ times the expected number of coordinates whose flip changes the value of $f$.
\end{theorem}

\proofstep
  {FABL.biasedFlipProbability}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p046-b002,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b003}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $p\in(0,1)$, let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$, and
let $i$ be a coordinate. The probability, under the product distribution with bias
parameter $p$, that flipping coordinate $i$ changes $f$ equals the mean under that same
distribution of the square of the discrete derivative of the real-valued sign function
associated to $f$ in coordinate $i$.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedSignPMF}
  {direct}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b003}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $p\in(0,1)$, let $f:\{ -1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$, and let
$i$ be a coordinate. The biased Fourier coefficient of $f$ on $\{i\}$ equals $\sigma_p$
times the product-distribution mean of its discrete derivative in coordinate $i$, where
$\sigma_p=\sqrt{4p(1-p)}$ and the discrete derivative is half the difference between the
values with that coordinate set to $1$ and to $-1$.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.biasedFlipProbability}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b002}
\proofstep
  {FABL.productInfluence_biased_eq_sigma_sq_mul_flipProbability}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b002,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b003}
\proofstep
  {FABL.biasedFlipProbability_eq_expect_sq_discreteDerivative}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b004,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b002}
\proofstep
  {FABL.biasedFourierCoeff_singleton_eq_sigma_mul_expect_discreteDerivative}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p221-b002,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b005}
Let $p\in(0,1)$, let $f$ be a monotone function from the $n$-dimensional sign cube to
the two signs, and let $i$ be a coordinate. Under the product distribution in which each
sign has bias parameter $p$, the influence of $f$ at coordinate $i$ equals
$\sqrt{4p(1-p)}$ times the biased Fourier coefficient of its real-valued sign
representation indexed by the singleton $\{i\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Edges on a finite vertex set]
\lean{FABL.GraphEdge}
\label{FABL.GraphEdge}
\leanok
For a natural number $v$, an edge on the vertex set $\{0,1,\ldots,v-1\}$ is a subset
containing exactly two vertices.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Boolean encoding of a graph]
\lean{FABL.EncodedGraph}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b005}
\label{FABL.EncodedGraph}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.GraphEdge}
For a natural number $v$, an encoded graph on the vertex set $\{0,1,\ldots,v-1\}$ is a
Boolean-valued function on the set of its two-element vertex subsets; the value records
whether each such pair is an edge.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Permutation of graph edges]
\lean{FABL.graphEdgePermEquiv}
\label{FABL.graphEdgePermEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.GraphEdge}
For a natural number $v$, let a graph edge be a two-element subset of $\in{v}$. Every
permutation $\sigma$ of $\in{v}$ induces a bijection on graph edges by sending each edge
to its image under $\sigma$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Relabeling an encoded graph]
\lean{FABL.permuteEncodedGraph}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b005}
\label{FABL.permuteEncodedGraph}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.EncodedGraph, FABL.graphEdgePermEquiv}
Let $v$ be a natural number, let $\sigma$ be a permutation of the vertex set
$\{0,1,\ldots,v-1\}$, and let $G$ be an encoded graph on that set. The relabeled graph
assigns to each pair of vertices the edge status in $G$ of the pair obtained by applying
$\sigma^{-1}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Invariant graph property]
\lean{FABL.IsGraphProperty}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p019-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b005
}
\label{FABL.IsGraphProperty}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.EncodedGraph, FABL.permuteEncodedGraph}
For a natural number $v$, a Boolean-valued graph property on the $v$-vertex set is
invariant under relabeling if its value is unchanged when the vertices are permuted, for
every permutation and every encoded graph.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Inclusion of encoded graphs]
\lean{FABL.EncodedGraphLE}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p224-b001}
\label{FABL.EncodedGraphLE}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.EncodedGraph}
For a natural number $v$ and encoded graphs $G,H$ on the $v$-vertex set, write $G\le H$
when every pair that is an edge of $G$ is also an edge of $H$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Monotone graph property]
\lean{FABL.IsMonotoneGraphProperty}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p224-b001}
\label{FABL.IsMonotoneGraphProperty}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.EncodedGraph, FABL.EncodedGraphLE}
For a natural number $v$, a Boolean-valued graph property on the $v$-vertex set is
monotone if whenever $G\le H$ and the property holds for $G$, it also holds for $H$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Number of encoded graph edges]
\lean{FABL.encodedGraphEdgeCount}
\label{FABL.encodedGraphEdgeCount}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.EncodedGraph}
Let $v$ be a natural number, and let $G$ assign a Boolean value to each two-element
subset of $\in{v}$. The encoded edge count of $G$ is the number of these subsets on
which $G$ takes the value true.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Edge count under vertex relabeling]
\lean{FABL.encodedGraphEdgeCount_permute}
\label{FABL.encodedGraphEdgeCount_permute}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.EncodedGraph, FABL.encodedGraphEdgeCount, FABL.graphEdgePermEquiv, FABL.permuteEncodedGraph}
\difficulty{3}
Let $v$ be a natural number, let $G$ assign a Boolean value to each two-element subset
of the $v$ vertices, and let $\sigma$ be a permutation of the vertices. The number of
edges of the relabeled graph equals the number of edges of $G$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Edge majority property]
\lean{FABL.edgeMajorityGraphProperty}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b006}
\label{FABL.edgeMajorityGraphProperty}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.EncodedGraph, FABL.GraphEdge, FABL.encodedGraphEdgeCount}
Let $G$ be a graph encoded by assigning a Boolean value to each edge on
$\{0,1,\ldots,v-1\}$. The edge majority property holds exactly when the total number of
possible edges is at most twice the number of edges assigned value true.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Edge majority is invariant under relabeling]
\lean{FABL.edgeMajority_isGraphProperty}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b006
}
\label{FABL.edgeMajority_isGraphProperty}

\proofstep
  {FABL.edgeMajorityGraphProperty}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b006,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b005}
For every natural number $v$, the Boolean property of a graph on $v$ vertices that
declares the graph to have edge majority when the total number of possible edges is at
most twice the number of present edges is invariant under every permutation of the
vertices.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Edge parity property]
\lean{FABL.edgeParityGraphProperty}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b006}
\label{FABL.edgeParityGraphProperty}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.EncodedGraph, FABL.encodedGraphEdgeCount}
Let $G$ be a graph encoded by assigning a Boolean value to each edge on
$\{0,1,\ldots,v-1\}$. The edge parity property holds exactly when the number of edges
assigned value true is odd.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Edge parity is invariant under relabeling]
\lean{FABL.edgeParity_isGraphProperty}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b006
}

  {FABL.edgeParityGraphProperty}
  {context}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b006}
For every natural number $v$, the Boolean property of a graph on $v$ vertices that
declares the graph to have odd many present edges is invariant under every permutation
of the vertices.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Biased Boolean probability mass function]
\lean{FABL.biasedBoolPMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p017-b007,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b003
}
\label{FABL.biasedBoolPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasedSignPMF}
For $p\in[0,1]$, take a sign with the biased sign probability mass function at parameter
$p$ and map it to a Boolean value that is true exactly when the sign is $-1$. The
resulting probability mass function on Boolean values is the biased Boolean probability
mass function at parameter $p$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Erdős–Rényi graph distribution]
\lean{FABL.erdosRenyiPMF}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p016-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b005
}
\label{FABL.erdosRenyiPMF}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.EncodedGraph, FABL.GraphEdge, FABL.biasedBoolPMF, FABL.independentProductPMF}
For a natural number $v$ and $p\in[0,1]$, assign each possible edge on
$\{0,1,\ldots,v-1\}$ an independent Boolean value, each with the biased Boolean
probability mass function at parameter $p$. The resulting probability mass function on
encoded graphs is the Erdős–Rényi graph distribution.
\end{definition}

  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b005}
Let $v$ be a nonnegative integer, and let $P$ be a Boolean-valued property of graphs on
$v$ vertices that is invariant under every permutation of the vertices. Then for every
vertex permutation and every encoded graph $G$, the property has the same value on the
permuted graph as on $G$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Biased mean of a sign monomial]
\lean{FABL.productMean_biasedSignPMF_monomial}
\label{FABL.productMean_biasedSignPMF_monomial}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.monomial, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_biasedSignPMF_signValue, FABL.pmfExpectation_const, FABL.pmfExpectation_independentProductPMF_prod, FABL.productMean, FABL.productProbabilityPMF, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $p\in[0,1]$, and let $S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$.
Under the product distribution of independent signs for which the probability of $-1$ is
$p$, the mean of the sign monomial indexed by $S$ is $(1-2p)^{|S|}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Biased expectation polynomial]
\lean{FABL.biasedExpectationPolynomial}
\label{FABL.biasedExpectationPolynomial}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff}
For a function $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ and a real parameter $\mu$, define the biased
expectation polynomial by $\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}\mu^{|S|}\widehat f(S)$, where
$\widehat f(S)$ is the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Biased expectation and product mean]
\lean{FABL.biasedExpectationPolynomial_biasMean}
\label{FABL.biasedExpectationPolynomial_biasMean}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasedExpectationPolynomial, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourier_expansion, FABL.monomial, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_const_mul, FABL.pmfExpectation_sum, FABL.productMean, FABL.productMean_biasedSignPMF_monomial, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $p\in[0,1]$, and let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$.
The biased expectation polynomial of $f$, evaluated at the bias mean $1-2p$, equals the
mean of $f$ under the product distribution on sign vectors whose coordinates have the
biased sign distribution with parameter $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Derivative of the biased expectation polynomial]
\lean{FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedExpectationPolynomial}
\label{FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedExpectationPolynomial}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasedExpectationPolynomial, FABL.fourierCoeff}
\difficulty{3}
For every real-valued function $f$ on $\{-1,1\}^n$ and every real number $\mu$, the
biased expectation polynomial $P_f(\mu)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\mu^{|S|}\widehat f(S)$
is differentiable at $\mu$ with derivative
$\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}|S|\mu^{|S|-1}\widehat f(S)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mean of a biased discrete derivative]
\lean{FABL.productMean_biasedSignPMF_discreteDerivative}
\label{FABL.productMean_biasedSignPMF_discreteDerivative}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.discreteDerivative, FABL.discreteDerivative_eq_fourier_sum, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.monomial, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_const, FABL.pmfExpectation_const_mul, FABL.pmfExpectation_sum, FABL.productMean, FABL.productMean_biasedSignPMF_monomial, FABL.productProbabilityPMF}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $0<p<1$, let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\mathbb R$, and choose a
coordinate $i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. Under the product distribution of independent signs
for which the probability of $-1$ is $p$, the mean of the discrete derivative of $f$ in
coordinate $i$ is $\displaystyle\sum_{S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\},\ i\in S}\widehat
f(S)(1-2p)^{|S|-1}$, where $\widehat f(S)$ is the uniform Fourier coefficient of $f$ at
$S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Biased derivative sum and Fourier coefficients]
\lean{FABL.sum_productMean_biasedSignPMF_discreteDerivative}
\label{FABL.sum_productMean_biasedSignPMF_discreteDerivative}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.discreteDerivative, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.productMean, FABL.productMean_biasedSignPMF_discreteDerivative}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $0<p<1$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function on
the $n$-dimensional sign cube. Give each coordinate an independent sign with probability
$p$ of being negative, and write $D_i f$ for the difference between the values of $f$
with coordinate $i$ set to $1$ and to $-1$, divided by $2$. Then
\[\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[D_i f]=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}} |S|(1-2p)^{\max(|S|-1,0)}\widehat f(S),\]
where $\widehat f(S)$ is the uniform Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Derivative via singleton Fourier coefficients]
\lean{FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedExpectationPolynomial_eq_singletons}
\label{FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedExpectationPolynomial_eq_singletons}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasSigma, FABL.biasSigma_pos, FABL.biasedExpectationPolynomial, FABL.biasedFourierCoeff, FABL.biasedFourierCoeff_singleton_eq_sigma_mul_expect_discreteDerivative, FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedExpectationPolynomial, FABL.sum_productMean_biasedSignPMF_discreteDerivative}
\difficulty{4}
Let $p\in(0,1$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function on $\{-1,1\}^n$. The biased
expectation polynomial $P_f$ is differentiable at $1-2p$, with derivative
$\sigma(p)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\widehat f_p(\{i\})$, where $\sigma(p)=\sqrt{4p(1-p)}$
and $\widehat f_p$ denotes the Fourier coefficient for the biased product measure with
parameter $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Biased probability of a negative output]
\lean{FABL.biasedMinusProbability}
\label{FABL.biasedMinusProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.productMean}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $p\in[0,1]$, and let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$. The
biased minus probability of $f$ is the expectation, under the product distribution on
sign vectors with bias parameter $p$, of the indicator that $f(x)=-1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Polynomial biased probability of a negative output]
\lean{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\label{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasedExpectationPolynomial}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$, and let $p\in\mathbb R$. The
polynomial biased minus probability of $f$ at $p$ is $(1-E_f(m(p)))/2$, where $E_f$ is
the biased expectation polynomial associated with the real-valued version of $f$, and
$m(p)$ is the bias mean corresponding to $p$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Product mean to real eq one sub two mul minus probability]

\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b003}
\label{FABL.productMean_toReal_eq_one_sub_two_mul_minusProbability}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.pmfExpectation_add_fun, FABL.pmfExpectation_const, FABL.pmfExpectation_smul_fun, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}

Statement pending regeneration.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial equals biased minus probability]
\lean{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq}
\label{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.biasedExpectationPolynomial_biasMean, FABL.biasedMinusProbability, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.productMean, FABL.productMean_toReal_eq_one_sub_two_mul_minusProbability, FABL.productProbabilityPMF, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $p\in[0,1]$, and let $f$ be a Boolean function on the
$n$-dimensional sign cube. The biased minus-probability polynomial of $f$ at $p$ equals
the probability that $f$ takes the value $-1$ under the product distribution with the
corresponding bias.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Derivative of the biased minus-probability polynomial]
\lean{FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\label{FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasSigma, FABL.biasedExpectationPolynomial, FABL.biasedFourierCoeff, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedExpectationPolynomial_eq_singletons}
\difficulty{4}
Let $p\in(0,1)$ and let $f$ be a function from $\{-1,1\}^n$ to $\{-1,1\}$. The
polynomial $Q_f(p)=(1-P_{f_{\mathbb R}}(1-2p))/2$, where $f_{\mathbb R}$ is the
real-valued sign representation of $f$, is differentiable at $p$ with derivative
$\sigma(p)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\widehat {f_{\mathbb R}}_p(\{i\})$, where
$\sigma(p)=\sqrt{4p(1-p)}$ and the coefficients are for the biased product measure
with parameter $p$.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}

  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p224-b003,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p225-b001}
Let $p\in(0,1)$, and let $f$ be a monotone function from $\{-1,1\}^n$ to
$\{-1,1\}$. The biased minus-probability polynomial $Q_f$ is differentiable at $p$
with derivative $\mathrm{Inf}_p(f)/\sigma(p)^2$, where $\mathrm{Inf}_p(f)$ is the
total influence of the real-valued sign representation of $f$ under the biased product
measure with parameter $p$, and $\sigma(p)=\sqrt{4p(1-p)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Biased variance bounded by total influence]
\lean{FABL.productVariance_le_productTotalInfluence_biased}
\label{FABL.productVariance_le_productTotalInfluence_biased}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.FiniteFourierBasis.fourierCoeff, FABL.FiniteFourierBasis.productTotalInfluence_eq_sum_order_mul_sq_fourierCoeff, FABL.FiniteFourierBasis.variance_eq_sum_sq_fourierCoeff, FABL.FiniteFourierBasis.zeroMultiIndex, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.biasedSiteFourierBasis, FABL.multiIndexOrder, FABL.multiIndexSupport, FABL.productTotalInfluence, FABL.productVariance}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$, and let $0<p<1$. Under
the product distribution on signs with $\Pr[X_i=-1]=p$ independently for each
coordinate, the variance of $f$ is at most its total product influence.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Positive variance of a nonconstant Boolean function]
\lean{FABL.productVariance_biased_pos_of_nonconstant}
\label{FABL.productVariance_biased_pos_of_nonconstant}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.PMFHasFullSupport, FABL.ProductL2, FABL.Sign, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.biasedSignPMF_hasFullSupport, FABL.pmfExpectation_nonneg, FABL.pmfInner, FABL.pmfInner_eq_expect, FABL.pmfInner_self_eq_zero_iff, FABL.productMean, FABL.productProbabilityPMF, FABL.productProbabilityPMF_hasFullSupport, FABL.productVariance, FABL.signValue, FABL.signValue_injective}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{\pm1\}$ be nonconstant. For
every $p$ with $0<p<1$, the variance of $f$ under the product distribution on signs with
$\Pr[X_i=-1]=p$ independently for each coordinate is strictly positive.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Positive biased total influence]
\lean{FABL.productTotalInfluence_biased_pos_of_nonconstant}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p225-b003}
\label{FABL.productTotalInfluence_biased_pos_of_nonconstant}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.productTotalInfluence, FABL.productVariance_biased_pos_of_nonconstant, FABL.productVariance_le_productTotalInfluence_biased}
\difficulty{1}
Let $p\in(0,1)$ and let $f$ be a sign-valued function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube.
If $f$ is nonconstant, then its total influence under the product distribution with bias
parameter $p$ is strictly positive.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Continuity of the biased minus-probability polynomial]
\lean{FABL.continuous_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\label{FABL.continuous_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasedExpectationPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f$ be a Boolean-valued function on the sign cube
$\{-1,1\}^n$. For each real $p$, form the polynomial $(1-P_f(1-2p))/2$, where
$P_f(\mu)=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}\mu^{|S|}\widehat f(S)$ and $\widehat
f(S)$ is the uniform Fourier coefficient of the real-valued sign representation of $f$.
This function of $p$ is continuous on $\bbr$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Strict increase of biased minus probability]
\lean{FABL.strictMonoOn_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p225-b003}
\label{FABL.strictMonoOn_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasSigma_pos, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.continuous_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.hasDerivAt_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq_totalInfluence, FABL.productTotalInfluence_biased_pos_of_nonconstant}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ be monotone in the coordinatewise order and nonconstant.
For $p\in[0,1]$, form the polynomial
$Q_f(p)=\frac{1-\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}(1-2p)^{|S|}\widehat f(S)}{2}$, where
$\widehat f(S)$ is the uniform Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S$. Then $Q_f$ is strictly
increasing on $[0,1]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Strict monotonicity of the biased minus probability]
\lean{FABL.biasedMinusProbability_strictMono}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p225-b003}
\label{FABL.biasedMinusProbability_strictMono}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasedMinusProbability, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq, FABL.strictMonoOn_biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial}
\difficulty{1}
Let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ be monotone and nonconstant. For $p,q\in[0,1]$ with $p<q$,
choose each coordinate independently to equal $-1$ with probability $p$ or $q$,
respectively. Then the probability that $f$ equals $-1$ under parameter $p$ is strictly
less than under parameter $q$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Extreme values of a nonconstant monotone function]
\lean{FABL.monotone_nonconstant_extreme_values}
\label{FABL.monotone_nonconstant_extreme_values}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.Sign, FABL.neg_one_le_sign, FABL.sign_eq_neg_one_of_le_neg_one, FABL.sign_eq_one_of_one_le, FABL.sign_le_one}
\difficulty{5}
Let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ be monotone and nonconstant. Then $f((-1,\ldots,-1))=-1$
and $f((1,\ldots,1))=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Endpoint values of the biased probability polynomial]
\lean{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_endpoints}
\label{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_endpoints}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.Sign, FABL.biasMean, FABL.biasedExpectationPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourier_expansion, FABL.monomial, FABL.monotone_nonconstant_extreme_values, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant function from
the $n$-dimensional sign cube to $\{\pm1\}$. The biased minus-probability polynomial
associated with $f$ equals $0$ at parameter $p=0$ and equals $1$ at parameter $p=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Complementary critical probability]
\lean{FABL.criticalComplement}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p226-b003}
\label{FABL.criticalComplement}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.criticalProbability}
Let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional cube, and let
$p_c$ denote its critical probability. The complementary critical probability is
$1-p_c$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Mean at the critical probability]
\lean{FABL.criticalMean}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p226-b003}
\label{FABL.criticalMean}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasMean, FABL.criticalProbability}
Let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional cube, and let
$p_c$ denote its critical probability. The critical mean is the bias mean at parameter
$p_c$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Standard deviation at the critical probability]
\lean{FABL.criticalSigma}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p226-b003}
\label{FABL.criticalSigma}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.biasSigma, FABL.criticalProbability}
Let $f$ be a monotone, nonconstant Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional cube, and let
$p_c$ denote its critical probability. The critical standard deviation is the bias
standard deviation at parameter $p_c$.

  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p222-b002}
For every natural number $m$, consider majority on sign vectors of length $2m+1$: it
returns $1$ when the sum of the coordinates is nonnegative and $-1$ otherwise. The mean
of this function under the uniform product distribution on the sign cube is zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniformity at half bias]
\lean{FABL.biasedSignPMF_one_half_eq_uniform}
\label{FABL.biasedSignPMF_one_half_eq_uniform}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.biasedSignPMF_apply_toReal, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{4}
At $p=\tfrac12$, the biased sign distribution on $\{\pm1\}$ is the uniform probability
distribution.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Majority at the unbiased parameter]
\lean{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_majority_one_half}
\label{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_majority_one_half}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.Sign, FABL.biasedMinusProbability, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_eq, FABL.biasedSignPMF, FABL.biasedSignPMF_one_half_eq_uniform, FABL.majority, FABL.pmfExpectation, FABL.productMean_toReal_eq_one_sub_two_mul_minusProbability, FABL.productMean_uniform_majority_odd_eq_zero, FABL.productProbabilityPMF, FABL.signValue, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{5}
For every nonnegative integer $m$, the biased-minus probability polynomial of majority
on $2m+1$ coordinates, evaluated at $p=1/2$, equals $1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nonconstancy of odd-dimensional majority]
\lean{FABL.majority_odd_isNonconstant}
\label{FABL.majority_odd_isNonconstant}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.majority, FABL.majority_unanimous}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $m$, the majority function on $\{-1,1\}^{2m+1}$ is nonconstant.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Critical probability of odd majority]
\lean{FABL.criticalProbability_majority_odd}
\label{FABL.criticalProbability_majority_odd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial, FABL.biasedMinusProbabilityPolynomial_majority_one_half, FABL.criticalProbability, FABL.existsUnique_criticalProbability, FABL.majority, FABL.majority_monotone, FABL.majority_odd_isNonconstant}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $m$, the critical probability of majority on $2m+1$ signs is
$\frac12$.
\end{theorem}
